text: Artificial intelligence can fake a voice, a face, a video, or a screenshot, cheaply and convincingly.
You probably already know this, but knowing fakes exist isn't a skill.
It doesn't tell you what to do in the 10 seconds after a suspicious clip hits your feed.
A friend sends you a video of your school principal announcing that classes are canceled for the entire next week.
This chart compares how we evaluate media across two eras.
Before artificial intelligence, the first question was, does it look real?
You would study the face, listen to the voice, and check the hallway in the background.
If you matched how the principal talks, you reached a verdict. The video is real.
In the AI era, that old test fails. The new question is, where is it from?
You ignore the pixels entirely and check the trail.
You skip studying the face and voice, and instead check the source that would actually know.
If nothing appears on the official school website, the claim remains unverified.
Appearance can mislead. The source trail can be checked.
The fake trap is believing a piece of media because it looks real.
It also has a second jaw, dismissing the actual truth because it could be a fake.
Sometimes a fake is just a joke. If a friend edits a picture of your hockey team hoisting the Stanley Cup,
everyone is in on the fun. There is no harm done.
The trap only begins when someone is meant to believe the illusion.
Harmful fakes are specifically engineered to extract something from you.
This graphic breaks down four goals behind harmful fakes.
Money. Outrage generates clicks and clicks pay.
Power. Changing beliefs influences how people vote and spend.
Fame. Viral clips bring followers without needing to be true.
Cruelty. Some fakes exist solely to humiliate an individual, particularly at school.
If you suspect a clip is malicious, your first instinct might be to upload it to an AI detector website to see if a machine made it.
An automated detector might flag a suspicious pattern, but it cannot make a final decision for you.
Because different tools often produce conflicting results, you have to look past the software and confirm the truth through your own independent investigation.
Fakes travel quickly when they spike your emotions.
If you feel a surge of outrage, fear, excitement, or hope, stop.
Run three specific checks before you react, share, or believe.
This panel shows our three checks.
The first check is source. Determine exactly who posted the content and ask if they have a way to know.
The second check is context.
Investigate what happened immediately before and after the event.
Identify crucial details that might be missing.
The third check is corroboration.
Search for an independent source that can confirm the exact same event or claim.
By applying these checks, you stop trying to spot fakes with your eyes.
You transfer the burden of proof onto verifiable external evidence.
Remember, another random account reposting the same viral clip does not count as independent confirmation.
There is one rule that supports every check.
You must verify information somewhere the sender does not control.
If a voicemail asks for something urgent, call back on the number you already have saved for them.
If a clip is blowing up online, look for the original source that would actually know the facts.
Until that trail checks out, unverified is your answer.
If a photo, clip, or account uses your name, do not handle it alone.
Save the username, the link, the date, and any messages when it is safe to do so.
Then bring in an adult that same day.
A parent, a counselor, or someone at school.
If someone shares a fake private image of a person under 18,
do not screenshot, download, or pass it around.
Tell a trusted adult immediately and reported through the platform.
NC mecs take it down and cyber tip line can also help.
Seeing or hearing isn't proof anymore.
Check the source, not the pixels.
